article.title: Why Overlap Matters Before You Trust a Propensity-Score Estimate
article.why: Distinguish covariate balance from empirical overlap and understand why both are needed.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: Austin PC — An Introduction to Propensity Score Methods

paragraphs.en:
Propensity-score methods are often evaluated by checking covariate balance after matching or weighting. If standardized mean differences become small, the adjusted treatment and control groups may look similar on observed characteristics. That is useful evidence, but it does not answer another crucial question: do the two groups actually have enough overlap to support the comparison?

The propensity score is the estimated probability of receiving treatment given observed covariates. Imagine a marketing program offered mainly to highly engaged customers. Many treated customers might have propensity scores near 0.95, while most untreated customers have scores below 0.30. A weighting method can try to compensate for this difference, but it cannot create abundant comparable untreated customers where almost none exist.

Overlap, sometimes discussed through positivity or common support, concerns whether units with relevant covariate profiles have a meaningful chance of appearing in both treatment conditions. If a certain type of customer is almost always treated, the data contain little direct information about what would have happened to that type without treatment.

This is different from balance. Balance asks whether the weighted or matched distributions of observed covariates are similar. Overlap asks whether the underlying data provide comparable observations in the first place. A procedure can produce attractive balance statistics by assigning very large weights to a few rare control observations. The SMDs may improve, yet the estimate becomes dependent on those few records.

Extreme weights are therefore an important warning sign. Suppose one untreated customer has a propensity score of 0.98. Under some inverse-probability weighting schemes, that observation may receive a very large weight because it represents many treated-like customers who are missing from the untreated group. The estimate may then become highly sensitive to a single unusual outcome.

Analysts should inspect propensity-score distributions by treatment group rather than relying only on a balance table. Histograms, density plots, or empirical distributions can reveal regions where one group has little or no support. Weight distributions and effective sample size provide additional diagnostics. A nominal sample of 100,000 observations may contain much less effective information after highly unequal weighting.

Poor overlap also affects the scientific question. If some customers are essentially always treated, estimating an average treatment effect for the entire population may require extrapolation beyond credible comparisons. One response is to redefine the target population to the region where both groups are represented. Depending on the estimand and method, analysts may use trimming, matching restrictions, overlap weights, or other approaches that reduce dependence on extreme observations.

These choices are not purely technical. Trimming customers with extreme propensity scores changes the population to which the result applies. An estimate for customers with good overlap may be more credible, but it should not be presented as an effect for every customer. The estimand and target population must be stated together.

Positivity also has a conceptual side. Structural lack of overlap occurs when treatment is impossible for some group by design. Random lack of overlap, by contrast, may improve with a larger sample. No statistical adjustment can manufacture a valid counterfactual in a region where the study design provides no comparison at all.

Good propensity-score analysis therefore uses several diagnostics together. Check covariate balance, overlap, the weight distribution, and effective sample size. Finally, examine whether the resulting target population still matches the business question. A small SMD is not a certificate that a causal estimate is trustworthy. Balance tells us whether the adjusted groups look similar; overlap tells us whether the comparison has enough empirical ground beneath it.
paragraphs.zh: Propensity-score 分析不能只看 weighting 或 matching 後的 SMD。Balance 問的是調整後兩組觀測特徵是否相似；overlap 則問資料本身是否存在足夠可比較的 treatment/control 個體。如果 treated 多集中在 propensity score 0.95 附近，而 control 幾乎都低於 0.30，少數罕見 control 可能被賦予極大權重，使 SMD 看似漂亮但估計高度依賴少數樣本。應同時檢查 propensity-score 分布、weight distribution、ESS 與 common support。若 trimming 或限制比較區域，target population 也會改變，結果不能再宣稱適用所有人。
paragraphs.ja: 傾向スコア分析では、重み付け後のSMDだけでなくoverlapも確認する必要があります。Balanceは調整後の属性分布が似ているかを問いますが、overlapはそもそも比較可能な処置群・対照群がデータ内に存在するかを問います。共通支持が乏しいと、少数の観測に極端な重みが付き、見かけ上のbalanceが良くても推定が不安定になります。傾向スコア分布、weight、ESSを併せて確認し、trimming等で対象を絞った場合は推定対象集団が変わることも明示します。

vocabulary.usage: Check overlap between treatment and control propensity scores.
Restrict analysis when common support is poor.
Extreme weights can make estimates unstable.
Choose a method that matches the estimand.
Trimming can reduce dependence on extreme scores.
Overlap supports a more credible counterfactual comparison.
Structural non-overlap may not improve with more data.

phrases.explanation: 有足夠資料實際支持某個比較。
phrases.example: We should confirm that this effect estimate has enough empirical support.

grammar.title: not only A but also B
grammar.body: 強調不能只做單一診斷，例如：Check not only balance but also overlap.

business.term: The SMDs look good, but do we have common support?
business.explanation: 在看到 balance 改善後進一步追問 overlap。
business.example: The SMDs look good, but do we have common support across the target population?

business.term: Which population does this estimate actually represent?
business.explanation: 確認 trimming 或 weighting 後真正的 estimand/target population。
business.example: After trimming extreme scores, which population does this estimate actually represent?

quiz.question: Can good covariate balance guarantee good overlap?
quiz.answer: No. A few heavily weighted observations can produce good balance while the underlying treatment and control distributions still have poor overlap.
